title: Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine I: Main Exam, 14 July 2026
unitTitle: Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine I
instructions: ATTEMPT ALL QUESTIONS IN SECTION A AND ANY OTHER TWO (2) IN SECTION B

items.text: SECTION A

The condition characterised by unilateral enlargement of one side of the face due to overgrowth of hard and soft tissues is called:
A. Micrognathia
B. Macrognathia
C. Hemifacial hypertrophy
D. Cleidocranial dysostosis

A small mandible is referred to as:
A. Micrognathia
B. Macrognathia
C. Prognathism
D. Retrognathia

The congenital anomaly characterised by the absence of the clavicles and delayed closure of the fontanelles is:
A. Cleft lip
B. Micrognathia
C. Cleidocranial dysostosis
D. Hemifacial hypertrophy

The visible yellow spots on the buccal mucosa near the commissures that represent ectopic sebaceous glands are called:
A. Fordyce's spots
B. Leukoplakia
C. Erythroplakia
D. Lichen planus

The fissured tongue condition characterised by multiple grooves on the dorsal surface is called:
A. Median rhomboid glossitis
B. Fissural tongue
C. Hairy tongue
D. Cleft tongue

A hereditary condition affecting enamel formation resulting in abnormal enamel that is soft, rough, or pitted is called:
A. Dentinogenesis imperfecta
B. Amelogenesis imperfecta
C. Enamel hypoplasia
D. Dental fluorosis

The most common supernumerary tooth found between the maxillary central incisors is the:
A. Paramolar
B. Distomolar
C. Mesiodens
D. Supplemental lateral incisor

A tooth that appears excessively large in size is described as:
A. Microdontia
B. Macrodontia
C. Fusion
D. Gemination

The developmental anomaly where a tooth has an abnormally long pulp chamber extending into the root is called:
A. Talon cusp
B. Dilaceration
C. Taurodontism
D. Odontome

An extra cusp projecting from the lingual surface of an anterior tooth is called:
A. Talon cusp
B. Cusp of Carabelli
C. Dens invaginatus
D. Dens evaginatus

The pathological wearing away of tooth structure due to tooth-to-tooth contact is called:
A. Abrasion
B. Attrition
C. Erosion
D. Abfraction

The loss of tooth structure caused by chemical dissolution (acid) not involving bacteria is called:
A. Attrition
B. Abrasion
C. Erosion
D. Abfraction

Excessive deposition of cementum on the root surface is called:
A. Hypercementosis
B. Cemental resorption
C. Cementoblastoma
D. Cemental hypoplasia

The most common fungal infection of the oral cavity is:
A. Herpes simplex
B. Actinomycosis
C. Candidosis
D. Tuberculosis

The causative organism of syphilis is:
A. Mycobacterium tuberculosis
B. Treponema pallidum
C. Streptococcus pyogenes
D. Candida albicans

A rapidly spreading, life-threatening infection involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces bilaterally is called:
A. Acute necrotising gingivitis
B. Ludwig's angina
C. Tuberculosis
D. Actinomycosis

The virus that causes chickenpox and shingles is:
A. Herpes simplex virus type 1
B. Herpes simplex virus type 2
C. Varicella-zoster virus
D. Coxsackie virus

The absence of a salivary gland is called:
A. Atresia
B. Agenesis
C. Aberrant tissue
D. Sialolithiasis

The presence of a stone (calculus) within a salivary gland duct is called:
A. Sialadenitis
B. Sialolithiasis
C. Ranula
D. Mucocele

A bluish, translucent swelling in the floor of the mouth caused by obstruction of the sublingual gland duct is called:
A. Mucocele
B. Ranula
C. Sialocele
D. Haemangioma

The autoimmune disorder characterised by dry mouth (xerostomia) and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) is:
A. Sicca syndrome
B. Lupus erythematosus
C. Scleroderma
D. Pemphigus vulgaris

A recurrent, painful, round ulcer with a yellow-grey centre and red halo, usually lasting 7-14 days, is called:
A. Herpetiform ulcer
B. Major aphthous ulcer
C. Minor aphthous ulcer
D. Traumatic ulcer

The definition of an ulcer is:
A. A raised solid lesion
B. A fluid-filled blister
C. A break in the epithelial continuity
D. A flat pigmented area

The condition where a tooth is bent or angulated due to trauma during root development is called:
A. Gemination
B. Fusion
C. Dilaceration
D. Concrescence

The union of two adjacent tooth germs resulting in a single large tooth is called:
A. Gemination
B. Fusion
C. Concrescence
D. Dens invaginatus

The most common site for a mucocele is:
A. Upper lip
B. Lower lip
C. Palate
D. Floor of mouth

The congenital condition characterised by a short lingual frenulum restricting tongue movement is called:
A. Cleft tongue
B. Ankyloglossia
C. Microglossia
D. Macroglossia

The reddish, smooth, depapillated area on the midline of the dorsal tongue is called:
A. Hairy tongue
B. Geographic tongue
C. Median rhomboid glossitis
D. Fissured tongue

Tetracycline staining of teeth occurs when the drug is taken during:
A. Adulthood
B. Tooth development
C. After tooth eruption
D. Old age

Acute necrotising gingivitis (ANG) is also known as:
A. Trench mouth
B. Thrush
C. Herpes simplex
D. Angular cheilitis
SECTION B
Discuss the developmental abnormalities affecting the dental hard tissues.
Discuss the common infections of the oral cavity.
Discuss salivary gland diseases and oral ulcerations.
